sections.title: Business Processes in Quality Inspection
sections.text:
3.1 Business Processes in Quality Inspection
Figure 3.1 illustrates a straightforward business process of quality inspection. The pro-
cess begins when the system automatically or a business user manually creates an
inspection lot 1, which is the beginning of the necessary quality inspection process.
The quality inspector records the inspection results 2, records any defects 3, and
makes a usage decision 4. The results recording step is the actual and factual data
entry of the results of each characteristic that is slated for an inspection. The inspection
results help you decide whether to use the material for further processing, such as in

3 Quality Inspection
110
procurement, production, or sales. The stock posting 5 is the last step in quality
inspection and determines whether the stock kept in quality inspection will be released
to unrestricted use, blocked, scrapped, or returned to the supplier. Several inspection
types aren’t stock-based; that is, no stock posting is required, and the quality inspec-
tion process ends with a usage decision only.
Figure 3.1 Inspection Lot Processing
We’ll discuss each in the following sections, though we’ll discuss defect recording after
the rest of the processes and use it to lead into the inspection report.

sections.title: Inspection Lot Creation
sections.text:
3.1.1 Inspection Lot Creation
When the system or the user creates an inspection lot in the system, the inspection lot
requires an inspection plan or material specification to calculate the sample size. This
sample size is then used for results recording and making a usage decision. However, if
the system is unable to calculate the sample size due to a missing or invalid inspection
plan or material specification, you can’t record results or make a usage decision for the
inspection lot.
To view the details of the inspection lot, use Transaction QA02 or menu path Logistics 
Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Inspection Lot Processing  Change. Figure
3.2 shows Inspection Lot 40000000653 of Material FG233, which the system automati-
cally creates at the end of the production process. Here, the process order (or produc-
tion order) against which the production took place is 700020.
One of the system statuses for the inspection lot 40000000653 is CHCR, which means
that the inspection plan (or material specification) is missing. As explained previously,
unless the system is able to assign an inspection plan to an inspection lot to calculate
its sample size, you can’t record results or make a usage decision.

In the following sections, we’ll look at the various elements of an inspection lot in
detail, including how to troubleshoot a missing inspection plan.
Assign Inspection Specifications
Choose the Inspection Specifications tab, shown in Figure 3.2, to go to the screen in
Figure 3.3. Here, the system automatically assigns the inspection plan with Usage 5 (if it
was created properly, which isn’t the case in our example). If an automatic assignment
isn’t possible, then the user can manually assign the inspection plan to an inspection
lot so that the sample size can be calculated. Usage 5 indicates that the inspection plan
is for goods receipt against a process, production, or purchase order. Because the sys-
tem was unable to find the inspection plan for Usage 5, the lower half of the Assigned
Specifications area is blank. Another possible reason could be a problem with the Key
Date. The system needs to find and be able to assign a valid inspection plan on the key
date. For example, say that during inspection plan creation, the key date is 04/27/
2024—but the key date that you see in Figure 3.3 is 02/27/2024. The system isn’t able to
assign an inspection plan with a key date that is later than the inspection lot creation
date. Hence, on this date (02/27/2024), the system is unable to find a relevant or active
inspection plan and is therefore unable to assign it to the inspection lot to calculate
sample size.

3 Quality Inspection

Figure 3.3 Unassigned Task List Specifications
Tips and Tricks
During an SAP S/4HANA implementation project, it’s generally a prudent practice to
agree to a key date that’s in the past for creating inspection plans of materials to avoid
the missing inspection plan error on the key date.
There are several options to troubleshoot and manually assign an inspection plan to
the inspection lot with a missing inspection plan:
 You can select a different material in the Material field and assign its inspection plan
to this inspection lot. For example, tea bags and tea packs are different materials, but
if they have the same inspection plan, you assign one to the other.
 You can also keep the Material the same (FG233) but use a different Plant for which
an inspection plan exists and assign that plant-specific inspection plan to this
inspection lot.
 You can select an inspection plan for the same material but a different usage and
assign it to this inspection lot. For example, if no inspection plan with usage 5 exists,
but one with usage 9 (material check) exists, you can enter it in the Usage field.
For this example, change or overwrite the key date to 03/27/2024, as shown in Figure 3.4,
and then choose the Task List/Spec. button. The system assigns the inspection plan with
the details shown in the Assigned Specifications area: Group 4 and Group Counter 2.

Whenever you or the system performs any business functions, the system automati-

text of the statuses, which you can display by choosing Extras  Inspection Lot Status or
clicking the blue icon located right next to the System Status field.

Figure 3.11 shows the SAP Fiori app Display Results History with the key figures such as
mean value, variance, and Cp and Cpk indices, along with associated graphs (both mean
values and single values). These values (of Cp and Cpk) are the process capability indi-
ces. The first value (Cp) is a measure for the process dispersion (is the process con-
trolled?), that is, how closely a process is running to its specification limits relative to
the natural variability of the process. The second value (Cpk) describes the position of
the mean value in relation to the tolerance limits and therefore indicates whether the
process is capable. The Cpk is an adjustment to the Cp, affecting its noncentered distri-
bution. In other words, Cpk measures how consistent the target values are with normal
performance. For a controlled and capable process, both values should be higher than
1.33. In many industries, the minimum requirement for a process capability index is
now 2.0 or higher! Details of Cpk and Cp are covered in Chapter 19.

sections.title: Usage Decision
sections.text:
3.1.3 Usage Decision
Now that results and defects (if any) are recorded for an inspection lot, the final steps
are to make a decision to use the material, which is known as the usage decision, and to
perform a stock posting of an inspection lot. The stock posting transfers the stock
placed in quality inspection into either an unrestricted-use stock or any other stock
type. The stock posting depends on the inspection type and inspection origin.
To record the usage decision of an inspection lot, use Transaction QA11 or follow menu
path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Inspection Lot  Usage Deci-
sion  Record. The screen that appears provides an option to enter a usage decision for a
single inspection lot. However, there are several other options available to efficiently
manage the task of performing a usage decision. The various icons (discussed in Sec-
tion 3.2) located in the menu bar are as follows:
 Mass Usage Decisions
This ensures that for all inspection lots for which the quality management (QM) user
needs to assign a single “accepted” code to several inspection lots, the user can do so
on a single screen and with one transaction.
 Quantity Posting Required
The entire activity of recording a usage decision stipulates two steps: the first step is
to assign a usage decision code to an inspection lot, and the second step is to per-
form stock posting. This option is available to business users; the usage decision
code is already assigned to an inspection lot (the first step is already performed), but

3 Quality Inspection
122
the user still needs to perform the important step of stock posting (the second step).
All such open inspection lot quantities are available in the form of a worklist to work
on.
 UD Not Taken Yet
This option brings up a complete worklist of all the inspection lots for which the QM
user needs to make usage decisions.
 Inspection Lots without Completion
This option offers a complete worklist of all inspection lots that are incomplete in
one form or another and are therefore open.
For this example, enter inspection lot “10000000702” and press (Enter) so that the
screen in Figure 3.14 appears. Here you see the Defects tab, which appears only when
the system records any defects during results recording. Moreover, you can also record
defects during a usage decision by choosing Defects located on the top menu bar or cre-
ate and activate a quality notification by choosing Notification. Defect recording is cov-
ered in detail in Section 3.1.5.
On this screen, choose the Characteristics tab to see the summarized results recording
available for evaluation before the user makes a usage decision. You can expand the
characteristic details by choosing All Characteristics.
Figure 3.14 Characteristics in Usage Decision
Select the box to the right of UD Code and press (F4) or choose the dropdown option.
The popup that appears provides a list of options available to the user to choose a usage
decision code. Each usage decision code valuates the inspection lot as either accepted
or rejected. The usage decision code also internally assigns a quality score to help in
© 

123
3.1 Business Processes in Quality Inspection
overall quality calculation of supplier-delivered material. These quality scores form the
basis of future procurement decisions with a supplier. Quality scores are automatically
updated with each usage decision. The relevant quality score isn’t shown until the user
selects the usage decision code.
Choose UD Code A, and the system automatically also assigns its associated catalog or
selected set, 01. With usage decision code A assigned, the system automatically assigns
the corresponding quality score of 100 (see Chapter 19 for more information on quality
scores).
Depending on the settings made in the material master, the system automatically cal-
culates and incorporates the shelf-life expiration date/best-before date (SLED/BBD), or
you can enter it manually. You also have the option to enter the long text of the usage
decision by choosing the Long Text icon located next to Code Valuation to enter any
additional details.

sections.title: Stock Posting
sections.text:
3.1.4 Stock Posting
In the Inspection Lot Stock tab shown in Figure 3.15, you enter the inspection lot quan-
tity into one of the several options available to perform the stock posting. These
options are as follows:
 To Unrestricted Use
The quantity placed in quality inspection is available as free to consume.
 To Scrap
The company destroys some or all of the quantity placed in quality inspection due
to the defective quality of the material. The scrapped quantity is charged to the rele-
vant cost center that you assigned in configuration.
 To Sample Consumptn
Either the system or the user can enter some quantity of material consumed as sam-
ples.
 To Blocked Stock
Some or all of the quantity placed in quality inspection is placed in blocked/
restricted-use stock. This stock isn’t available to use.
 To New Material
You can perform transfer posting of one material into another material after evalu-
ating that the material fits more with the new/different material than the original
material.
 To Reserves
You can assign some quantity to reserve stock for subsequent use.
 Return Delivery (not shown)
You decide to return complete or partial quantity to the supplier due to defective
quality or noncompliance with specifications.

3 Quality Inspection
124
Tips and Tricks
Right next to each stock type, you can choose details to view or change default infor-
mation. For example, you can choose the Document button (which will show Details
when you hover over it) of the To Scrap field and change the default cost center.
In Figure 3.15, the system shows that out of 100 PC of inspection lot quantity (Insp. Lot
Qty), you can post up to a quantity of 90 PC to unrestricted-use stock (or any other
stock type available), while the system automatically calculates the sample use of 100
PC.
Figure 3.15 Inspection Stock Posting
This sample calculation is based on the settings that you made for the relevant master
inspection characteristic. You can enter any combination here that reflects the actual
stock posting that you want to perform. For example, you can delete the sample-use
quantity of 10 PC, and post the entire 100 PC of inspection lot quantity to unrestricted-
use or blocked stock.
For this example, enter To Unrestricted Use as “90” and To Sample Consumptn as “10”.
Choose the Document button, and Figure 3.16 appears. If you need to change the docu-
ment or posting dates, then you can do so here; otherwise, this step is unnecessary.
© 

125
3.1 Business Processes in Quality Inspection
Figure 3.16 Usage Decision Header Data
If a material is batch-managed, then you can also change the batch status to restricted
or unrestricted, as deemed necessary. Otherwise, you can separately change the status
of a batch using Transaction MSC2N (Change Batch).

sections.title: Defect Recording
sections.text:
3.1.5 Defect Recording
During results recording, the quality inspector finds quite a few defects, and the need
to record these defects becomes evident for subsequent action by either returning the
defective material to the supplier or requesting replacement (or rework, in the case of
in-house-produced material). As already explained, you perform defects recording
during results recording and usage decision. Once a usage decision for an inspection
lot is made, you can no longer record defects.
To record defects, use Transaction QF11 or use menu path Logistics  Quality Manage-
ment  Quality Inspection  Defects  Record for Inspection Lot. On the initial screen that
appears, enter inspection lot “10000000701” and report type “00000010”. Whenever
a user enters the defects of an inspection lot, it’s mandatory for the user to choose the
relevant report type. A report type denotes that when the user runs the corresponding
defects reports in the system, the relevant information is available for display and
analysis purposes. Several standard defect report types are available, or you can config-
ure new report types to cater to any specific business processes (see more about report-
ing in Chapter 18). Some of the options available for report types are in several
combinations of defect types, number of defects, defect locations, causes of defect, and
activities for the QM user to perform on recording the defects.
Press (Enter), and the system offers three options through a popup to record the defect
data at the inspection-lot level, operation level, or master inspection characteristic
level. The defects recording at the inspection lot stipulates that the quality inspector
found the defects in the entire inspection lot. At the operation level, it’s the specific
operation or stage/phase in which the quality inspector found the defects. At the char-
acteristics level, it’s the particular master inspection characteristic for which the qual-
ity inspector intends to record defects.

3 Quality Inspection
126
Tips and Tricks
You can also use Transaction QF21 for operation defect recording and Transaction QF31
for characteristics defect recording.
Select the Inspection Lot radio button and then choose Continue, so that Figure 3.17
appears.
Figure 3.17 Defects Recording
To begin recording defects, first choose Defects from the top menu bar. In the popup
that appears, choose the Code Group column, and press (F4). A code group and its asso-
ciated codes represents the logical grouping of different defect types available in a cat-
alog. A few examples of different defect code groups and types of different defects in
pumps are combined together in one code group, and all types of electrical defects are
combined in one defect code group. All supplier-related defects, which the company
normally observes or handles, are grouped together in one defect code group, and all
the production-related defects on one machine or group of machines are combined
into one defect code group. The quality inspector can enter the number of defects
against each defect code. However, these defective quantities aren’t directly related to
or integrated with the inspection lot quantity or goods receipt quantity.
For this example, enter a Code group of “QM-E” and Code of “1” (Defect Type: Out of
Specification). When the user selects a defect code, the system automatically assigns a
defect class to it to categorize the nature of the defect. A defect class denotes the sever-
ity of the defect. Some of the defect classes are critical defect, major defect, and minor
defect. These defect classes are available as standard options in the system, but you can
also configure and make available new defect classes to meet your business needs.
© 

127
3.1 Business Processes in Quality Inspection
The user can also enter a short description for each defect code in the corresponding
Description column, as well as a long text. When the necessary entries are made, Figure
3.17 shows three defects along with other details such as the defect type, number of
defects for each defect type, and defect class.

sections.title: Inspection Report
sections.text:
3.1.6 Inspection Report
The inspection report displays the inspection results and comments of every charac-
teristic on the screen as a print preview or in the form of a printout. This means it can
also be used to provide an overview of the inspection carried out, or it can be referred
to as a basis for the usage decision. It can also serve as an attachment to a quality noti-
fication to the supplier or to internal departments to describe in detail the deviations
of individual characteristics according to type and scope, in the case of defects.
To display the inspection report, use Transaction QGA3 or follow menu path Quality
Management  Quality Inspection  Inspection Result  Print. The system displays the
Results Print selection screen. If you know the inspection lot number, you can enter it
directly. Otherwise, the selection allows you to set limits through known parameters
such as material number, supplier, and date, among others. Figure 3.18 shows an exam-
ple of a print preview (selective) of an inspection report for inspection lot 10000000701
for material RM17.

sections.title: Inspection Lot
sections.text:
3.2.2 Inspection Lot
Let’s now cover the inspection lot and its various business scenarios.
Correct Errors
To correct quantity-related errors of an inspection lot, use Transaction QAC1 or follow
menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Inspection Lot  Pro-
cessing  Lot Quantity  Correct Errors. You can use this option to correct or change both
stock-based and non-stock-based inspection lots. The stock-based quantity update is
especially helpful when the system automatically creates an inspection lot on receipt
of goods for a purchase or process order and accordingly suggests an inspection lot
quantity, which you can change, if needed.
Stock Transfer
Let’s say that you receive a quality stock of material, and on inspection, you conclude
that you need to keep it in a separate storage location or transfer it to a different plant.
In this case, you use the stock transfer option. When you use this option, the stock
that’s transferred to a different plant or storage location still remains in quality inspec-
tion until you record results, make a usage decision, and perform stock posting.
To transfer stock plant-to-plant or store-to-store for an inspection lot, use Transaction
QAC2 or follow menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Inspec-
tion Lot  Processing  Lot Quantity  Stock Transfer.
On the initial screen that appears, enter the stock of which you want to transfer-post in
the inspection lot, and press (Enter). The Transfer Posting Insp. Lot Stock area shows
the current location of the quality stock.
You can enter a different plant for stock for plant-to-plant stock transfer, or simply
keep the same plant (as in this example) and change the storage location of inspection
stock from 0001 to 0002 (see the St.Loc.ILotStock field) in the Stock Transfer Based On
area.
© 

131
3.2 Optimization Features of Inspection Planning and Quality Inspection
Cancel Sample Calculation
On inspection lot creation (manual or automatic), the system assigns an inspection
plan or material specification and calculates a sample size. If you realize that you or the
system incorporated an incorrect or obsolete inspection plan and therefore calculated
a wrong sample size, you can cancel the sample calculation. Canceling the sample cal-
culation also enables you to reassign a new or different inspection plan and accord-
ingly recalculate the sample size. In other words, you have to cancel the sample
calculation before the system allows you to reassign an inspection plan and then recal-
culate the sample size.
To cancel a sample calculation, use Transaction QAC3 or follow menu path Logistics 
Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Inspection Lot  Processing  Cancel Sample
Calculation. On the initial screen that appears, enter the inspection lot of the sample
you want to cancel, press (Enter), and then simply save.
Tips and Tricks
To cancel, you can also use Transaction QA02 (Change Inspection Lot); on the initial
screen, enter the inspection lot number, and choose Cancel Sample.
Inspection Lots with Outstanding Quantities
It’s of interest to the quality inspector to have a complete list of inspection lots for
which a usage decision may or may not be made, but for which stock posting is still
pending or outstanding. To access inspection lots with outstanding quantities and be
able to make usage decisions on the same screen, use Transaction QVM2 or follow
menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Worklist  Inspection
Lot Completion  Inspection Lot with Stock. In Figure 3.21, notice that the system sta-
tuses of a few inspection lots stipulate that the usage decision has already been made,
but its stock posting remains.
Figure 3.21 Outstanding Inspection Quantities

3 Quality Inspection
132
Tips and Tricks
Transaction QVM1 is for inspection lots with inspection completion, whereas Transac-
tion QVM3 is for inspection lots without a usage decision.
Cancel Inspection Lot
If you or the system has created an inspection lot that you no longer want to inspect or
use, you’ll want to cancel it. This option is helpful when you’ve mistakenly activated an
inspection type against which the system created an inspection lot. To cancel, first go
to Transaction QA02 (Change Inspection Lot), then navigate to Inspection Lot  Func-
tions  Cancel Lot. The system sets the status of the inspection lot to LTCA. Similarly, if
you want to reset an inspection lot cancellation, navigate to Inspection Lot  Functions 
Reset Cancellation.
Block Inspection Lot
To temporarily block an inspection lot so that you can perform additional tests, or to
prevent the quality inspector from making its usage decision or stock posting, you can
block the inspection lot. To do so, first go to Transaction QA02 (Change Inspection Lot),
and then navigate to Inspection Lot  Functions  Block Lot. The system sets the status of
the inspection lot to LKD. Similarly, to unblock an inspection lot, navigate to Inspection
Lot  Functions  Unblock Lot.

sections.title: Digital Signature
sections.text:
3.2.3 Digital Signature
The digital signature functionality reduces the number of printed documents that need
to be signed within an organization. You can define and then assign digital signatures in
an SAP system during various transaction processes, such as recording results and mak-
ing usage decisions in QM, changing the status of a document in Document Manage-
ment System (DMS), or completing a process instructions sheet in production planning
(PP). Digital signatures can be internal, such as an SAP system user’s password, or even
use external devices, such as fingerprint readers or card slides. Digital signatures can
confirm important business decisions in QM, such as according approval to the quality
inspection lot, validating the correctness of shift reports in plant maintenance (PM), or
simply confirming the values of process parameters in production planning for process
industries (PP-PI). They do all of this electronically, saving significant time and effort,
eventually bringing about improvements in business processes and saving money.
The following are some of the areas in QM in which you can integrate digital signatures
with relevant business processes:
 Inspection lot approval
 Results recording
© 

133
3.2 Optimization Features of Inspection Planning and Quality Inspection
 Usage decisions
 Physical-sample drawing
 Header or item level of QM notification
Note
Throughout this book, we’ve highlighted the business processes in which you can inte-
grate digital signatures.
It’s important to highlight that the digital signature configuration that you undertake
here for QM is directly assigned at the material level (we’ll show this later). Hence, from
the implementation consideration point of view, consider some or all of the preceding
combinations of business processes in which you’ll use the same digital signature
strategy. For example, will a material require a digital signature for approval of only the
inspection lot, or will it also need a digital signature at the time of results recording? If
the latter, then a combination of a single QM material authorization group that encom-
passes both the business processes (inspection lot approval and results recording) will
suffice. If the business process requires a digital signature on physical sample with-
drawal, then configuring a separate QM material authorization group to cater to this
business need and then assigning it to the material master serves the needed purpose.
Note
If you further integrate digital signature functionality with SAP Business Workflow,
then the person responsible for digitally signing a particular SAP system object auto-
matically receives the relevant information via the SAP system inbox.
This section begins by covering the important steps you need to take to configure dig-
ital signatures. Then, we’ll run the entire end-to-end business process in QM to show
how digital signatures work.
Note
The concepts and flows that we’ll cover for digital signatures in QM are equally appli-
cable to all the other areas of SAP S/4HANA that digital signatures apply to.
Configuration Basics
Following are the six important steps in configuring a digital signature:
1. Define authorization groups.
2. Define individual signatures.
3. Define a signature strategy.

3 Quality Inspection
134
4. Create authorization groups for QM master data.
5. Configure the material authorization group, inspection lot approval, digital signa-
ture.
6. Create a signature method.
Tips and Tricks
Although this section focuses on digital signatures in QM, the general menu path for
digital signatures is SAP IMG  Cross-Application Components  General Application
Functions  Digital Signature.
We’ll now discuss each of the steps for configuration in the following sections.
Define Authorization Groups
An authorization group is used to limit the authorization of a transaction or group of
transactions to a specific user or group of users performing the same role. Once config-
ured, this authorization group can be controlled through authorization object C_SIGN_
BGR. You need to coordinate with your SAP NetWeaver (Basis) team members to get the
right authorization group assigned to the right user.
To create an authorization group, follow SAP system menu path SAP IMG  Quality
Management  Environment  Central Functions  Signature Strategy  Define Authoriza-
tion Groups. Here, you can see the initial screen for the creation of an authorization
group for digital signatures (see Figure 3.22). Choose the New Entries button (not
shown) to create a new authorization group, UD, and enter a description (“Digital Signa-
ture for UD”, in this example). Save the authorization group.
Figure 3.22 Creating New Authorization Group
Define Individual Signatures
An individual signature is a unique identification in the SAP system to which a user is
assigned. To create a new individual signature, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality
Management  Environment  Central Functions  Signature Strategy  Define Individual
Signatures. In the screen that appears (see Figure 3.23), choose New Entries, and define
two individual signatures—UD01 and UD02—with descriptions.
© 

135
3.2 Optimization Features of Inspection Planning and Quality Inspection
Figure 3.23 Two Individual Signatures
Both individual signatures are assigned to the same authorization group—UD—as
shown in Figure 3.23. Save the entries.
Define a Signature Strategy
A signature strategy is the combination of different individual signatures that are
assigned to an authorization group. A signature strategy also defines the sequence and
flow of individual signatures and maintains the predecessor-successor relationships.
The signature strategy is used to control the level to which the document can be con-
sidered released. A Released status denotes that the digital signature process is com-
plete in every respect.
Tips and Tricks
If you don’t have a business need to configure and define a digital signature strategy,
then you can skip all the steps that we’ve covered in this section and move on to the
following sections. These digital signature settings are specific only to QM objects,
such as inspection lot approval, results recording, and usage decision.
To create a signature strategy, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Envi-
ronment  Central Functions  Signature Strategy  Define Signature Strategy (see Figure
3.24).
Figure 3.24 Signature Strategy

3 Quality Inspection
136
Before we show you how to create a new signature strategy, we need to explain some of
the columns in Figure 3.24 and their functions. The third column, Signature Method,
stipulates how the SAP system verifies a signature. The three possible options are as fol-
lows:
 System signature with authorization, using an SAP system username and password
 User signature with external security product with verification
 User signature with external security product without verification
The Comment column enables a user to enter comments when they execute the digital
signature. In the Remark column, users can enter a short text before signing. The Doc-
ument column is an option to allow or disallow viewing of a document. The Verifica-
tion column, with the checkbox, verifies the sequence of the digital signature, known
as the signature strategy, before the system marks the document as complete.
Choose the newly created SigStrat UD in Figure 3.24, and then choose Assign individual
signatures. Then, in Figure 3.25, maintain the entries of two individual signatures pre-
viously created in Figure 3.23.
To define a new signature strategy, choose New Entries at the top of the screen shown
in Figure 3.24.
Figure 3.25 Assigning Individual Signatures to a Signature Strategy
In the second screen of the same figure, define the signature strategy UD with the
description “Usage Decision Auth. Group”. Then, select System Signature and Password
to be the signature option, and make the Displ. Comment box, Display Remark box, and
Disp. Document required entries. Finally, select the Verify checkbox to require verifica-
tion of the signature strategy. Figure 3.26 shows the summary of all the settings made.
Next, select the signature strategy UD in the SigStrat field, and double-click the Assign
individual signatures folder. Choose New Entries (see Figure 3.26), and add the previ-
ously created individual signatures UD01 and UD02 to the signature strategy UD. Save
and then choose Back to return to the overview screen.
© 

137
3.2 Optimization Features of Inspection Planning and Quality Inspection
Figure 3.26 Signature Sequence of a Signature Strategy
Figure 3.24, shown earlier, displays the signature strategy overview screen, but now
with a new entry, UD. Select the newly created signature strategy, UD, and choose the
Signatures button on the right side.
Figure 3.27 shows the Release States of Signature St... screen, in which individual signa-
ture UD01 must be signed before individual signature UD02. In other words, UD01 is
the predecessor (denoted as the predecessor in the UD01 column), and UD02 is the suc-
cessor. Choose Continue to go to the screen shown previously in Figure 3.26.
Figure 3.27 Individual Signature for Signature Strategy
Select the signature strategy UD in Figure 3.26, and choose Release from the popup that
appears. Select the checkbox that denotes the release status of the document, as well as
the completion of the signature strategy. A completion strategy means that the
required sequence of digital signatures is ensured. For this example, select the checkbox

3 Quality Inspection
138
in the second row, in which both individual signatures, UD01 and UD02, must be marked
for the signature strategy to declare it as complete.
Choose Continue and save. The configuration needed to enable the SAP system digital
signature is complete. However, for the digital signature to work in the desired busi-
ness process, you need to assign the newly created signature strategy UD to the rele-
vant material master, which we’ll cover in the next section.
Create Authorization Groups for Quality Management Master Data
To create an authorization group for QM master data, follow menu path SAP IMG 
Quality Management  Environment  Central Functions  Authorization Management 
Define Authorization Groups and Digital Signature.
Choose the first option Authorization Group for QM Master Data. Choose New Entries,
define AuthGroup as UD000001, enter a Short Text description, and save (see Figure
3.28).
Figure 3.28 Authorization Group
Configure the Material Authorization Group, Inspection Lot Approval, and
Digital Signature
In Figure 3.29, choose New Entries to bring up the option to make detailed settings for
digital signature for some or all of the four QM objects: inspection lot approval, results
recording, usage decision, and physical sample drawing.
Let’s review the three available digital signature options for each of the four QM
objects:
 Not Required
There will be no need to digitally sign the QM object.
 Required for Making Digital Signature of the Object
This option provides for a single digital signature, with no provision to incorporate
a signature strategy (multiple digital signatures).
 Required for “New” Digital Signature
This option is used to select either a synchronous signature process (digitally sign-
ing the QM object only in the logical and sequential order) or an asynchronous sig-
nature process with and without a changeable signatory. Finally, in the last field,
© 

139
3.2 Optimization Features of Inspection Planning and Quality Inspection
which is Sig. (Signature) Strategy, you can enter the signature strategy that you’ve
already created in the previous steps in this chapter. In the case of synchronous sig-
nature selection, all users have to digitally sign the QM object one after the other
until the entire signature process is complete. In the case of the asynchronous
option, different users can digitally sign the QM object at different times.
Figure 3.29 QM Material Authorization
In this example, choose the Required for “New” Digital Signature option for results
recording. As soon as you do this, the system brings up the option to select the asyn-
chronous signature process with changeable history for signature type. Finally, enter
the signature strategy UD that you created previously.
In addition, for the usage decision, choose option 1, which requires a digital signature at
the time of making a usage decision.
Create a Signature Method
To create a signature method for QM master data, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality
Management  Environment  Central Functions  Authorization Management  Define
Authorization Groups and Digital Signature  Specify Signature Method for Approval
Using Simple Signature (see Figure 3.30). Here, first check whether the Object is already

3 Quality Inspection
140
available on the screen. If it’s available, then simply select the Signature Method as a
System Signature with an SAP username and password. If the signature object type
isn’t available, then you can choose New Entries and select the relevant object from the
large number of objects available for the signature method.
With this, we conclude the necessary digital signature configuration and proceed to
assigning the configured QM material authorization group in the material master.
Figure 3.30 Signature Method for Simple Signature
Digital Signature in Quality Management Business Processes
In this section, we’ll assign the configuration that we undertook for the digital signa-
ture. It’s only a single step of assigning the configured QM material authorization
group to the relevant material. Next, we create a manual inspection lot, record results
to see if the digital signature is correctly configured and available, and finally record a
usage decision to see if the digital signature pops up again (refer to the settings we
made in Figure 3.29).
Assigning the Quality Management Material Authorization Group in the Material Master
To assign the QM authorization group UD0001, use Transaction MM02, enter material
number “RM17” in the Material field, and select the Quality management view. On the
Organizational Levels prompt (not shown), enter plant “1710”, and then press (Enter).
© 

141
3.2 Optimization Features of Inspection Planning and Quality Inspection
The screen in Figure 3.31 appears. In the QMatAu field, choose the just configured
option UD0001 from the dropdown menu shown on the right side of the screen, and
save the settings.
Figure 3.31 Assignment of QM Material Authorization in the Material Master
Tips and Tricks
You can also use the QM Material Auth.. field in Figure 3.31 to control authorization of
who is allowed to perform necessary business functions. For example, you have one
group of quality inspectors who are responsible for inspecting raw and packaging
materials. You have another group of quality inspectors who inspect semifinished and
finished goods. To restrict relevant inspectors to performing QM tasks such as results
recording and usage decisions that are specific to their material type (e.g., raw materi-
als or finished goods), you can create two different authorization groups and assign
them in the QM Material Auth. field of the relevant material masters. Then, also assign
these objects to the individual inspectors’ user profiles to restrict their authorizations
and working rights.
We suggest that you engage a Basis/SAP NetWeaver consultant to restrict authoriza-
tions.
Inspection Lot Creation
To create a new manual inspection lot, use Transaction QA01; on the initial screen,
enter Material “RM17”, Plant “1710”, and Inspection Type “89” (for manual inspection).

3 Quality Inspection
142
On the inspection lot creation screen, enter the inspection lot quantity as “10”, and save
the inspection lot. The system creates an inspection lot and assigns an internal inspec-
tion lot number, which in this example is 10000000704.
Digital Signature in Results Recording
To record results, use Transaction QE01, and enter the same inspection lot number,
“10000000704”, and its operation, “0010”.
Figure 3.32 shows that after entering the results of inspection lot 10000000704, the
system brings up the popup window for you to digitally sign. Here, enter the short text,
the signatory, and the SAP system password. On successful completion of the digital
signature, the system displays an information message at the bottom of the screen.
Figure 3.32 Digital Signature Popup during Results Recording
Digital Signature in Usage Decision
On successful completion of results recording and digitally signing the results, use
Transaction QA11 to record the usage decision of the same inspection lot,
10000000704. As soon as you enter the usage decision code and save, the system
prompts you to enter the SAP system password. This process is exactly the same as that
covered in the previous section.
Digital Signature Logs
The SAP system provides a comprehensive log that you can view to ensure complete
visibility of all the activities undertaken for digital signatures.
© 

143
3.2 Optimization Features of Inspection Planning and Quality Inspection
Note
This digital signature log is also available in all the applications and areas in which dig-
ital signatures are used, which includes PM, QM, engineering change management,
and PP-PI.
To access the digital signature logs, use Transaction DSAL or follow menu path Quality
Management  Quality Inspection  Info System  Digital Signature  Logs. This takes you
to the initial screen to enter relevant parameters.
In the Applic. (application) field, choose LOT (Inspection Lot); in the lower half of the
screen, under the Inspection Lot tab, enter the inspection lot as “10000000704”. Press
(F8) or choose Execute. The screen in Figure 3.33 provides a comprehensive log of digi-
tal signatures for inspection lot 10000000704.
Figure 3.33 Digital Signature Log
The bottom half of the screen provides details about who executed the digital signa-
tures and when. It also provides details of the individual signatures (UD01 and UD02),
as well the signature strategy UD. Further, the system also maintains a complete log of
all attempts, whether successful or not, to digitally sign an object. Notice that in the
upper half of the same figure, there are a few red dots on the left side, which denotes an
unsuccessful attempt to digitally sign inspection lot 10000000703.
Tips and Tricks
To access the digital signature worklist, use Transaction QEDS or follow menu path
Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Worklist  Signature Process.

3 Quality Inspection
144

sections.text:
3.2.4 Results Recording
Let’s now cover results recording and its various business scenarios—specifically,
copying inspection results of one inspection lot to another as well as copying inspec-
tion results into batch classification.
Copy Inspection Results of an Inspection Lot
The SAP S/4HANA system provides an option to copy inspection results of an inspec-
tion lot into subsequent inspection lots, based on the configuration and master data
settings, which we’ll cover in the following sections. The configuration settings are
inspection-type-specific for a particular plant in which available copy controls are at
the inspection-lot-creation level and at the results-recording level. You can copy the
inspection results during inspection lot creation or results recording.
While this functionality is more commonly used in recurring inspections (inspection
type 09), you can also use this functionality for any other inspection type/plant combi-
nation, as this example shows.
Configuration Settings
To set up the necessary configuration settings for copying inspection results, follow
menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Results Recording 
Make Settings for Copy of Inspection Results. Review Figure 3.34 and Figure 3.35
together: these are part of the same screen, in which you copy inspection results set-
tings. This example shows configuration settings of inspection type 89 (manual inspec-
tion) for plant 1710.
Figure 3.34 Copy Inspection Results: Screen 1
Table 3.3 explains the fields and settings of Figure 3.34 and Figure 3.35.
© 

145
3.2 Optimization Features of Inspection Planning and Quality Inspection
Figure 3.35 Copy Inspection Results: Screen 2
Field Column Details
Inspection Type Inspection type to which copy inspection results are applicable.
Plant Plant of the inspection type for which the copy inspection results
apply.
Control in Insp. Lot
(inspection lot)
Option to control the mode of data transfer or data copy. The
available options are as follows:
 No data transfer at the inspection-lot-creation level
 Automatic data transfer on sample calculation
 Manual and automatic data transfer
In the case of manual data transfer, the system prompts you to
enter the inspection lot number of the data that you want to
copy or transfer (see Figure 3.34).

Option to control the mode of data transfer or data copy. The

Master Data Setup
After configuration settings are in place, you need to make a single master data setting
for the master inspection characteristics in the inspection plan of the material-plant
combination to define the data origin to copy inspection results from.
Figure 3.36 shows the inspection plan (Transaction QP02) for material RM17 and plant
1710. For Characteristic 10 of Activity 0010, choose Results Data Origin as 02 Previous

lot, you can choose to copy batch results of an inspection lot to the just-created inspec-
tion lot.
Let’s now delve into the business side of this process.
Figure 3.36 Origin of Results Data
Business Process of Copy Inspection Results
Figure 3.37 shows a previously created inspection lot 890000000350, with the results
of five characteristics, which you use as a reference to copy it to the next (or another)
inspection lot (see Figure 3.38).

Figure 3.37 Original Inspection Lot
Figure 3.38 Copy Results from Another Inspection Lot
Figure 3.38 shows the popup that prompts you to enter a reference inspection lot, the

Create a new inspection lot using Transaction QA01 for material RM17, plant 1710, and
inspection type 89. The system creates inspection lot number 890000000351, and the

popup prompts the user to enter the reference of the inspection lot to be used for copy-
ing results into the newly created inspection lot. For this example, enter inspection lot
number “890000000350”; the system displays the log shown in Figure 3.39.
Figure 3.39 shows the Display Logs screen of a successful (or unsuccessful) copy of

copied-to inspection lot 890000000351 in the External ID column. As you can see here,
it’s not possible to copy inspection results of a classed characteristic as well as that of a

Figure 3.39 Display Logs of Copied Inspection Results
Figure 3.40 shows that inspection lot 890000000351 comprises the copied results, and
the Origin is 02 Previous Inspection Lot, which you set up in the characteristic of the
inspection plan. If there is any specific or unique business need, you can still make

3 Quality Inspection
150
Figure 3.40 Inspection Results Copied from Previous Inspection Lot to New Inspection Lot
Access Figure 3.41, which is the results recording screen (Transaction QE01) of inspec-
tion lot number 890000000351. Because your configuration settings stipulate that
you can also use the manual option to copy inspection results, choose Edit  Copy
Inspection Results. When you do this, the system brings up the inspection lot selection
popup. Enter the previous (or other) inspection lot number, and choose Continue. The
system brings up operation(s) within the inspection lot for you to choose.
Figure 3.41 Copy Options for Results Recording
© 

151
3.2 Optimization Features of Inspection Planning and Quality Inspection
Copy Inspection Results into Batch Classification
Now that you’re familiar with how to manually or automatically copy inspection
results of one inspection lot to another, you can also copy inspection results into
batch classifications. In this business process, the results of an inspection lot are
directly transferred as characteristic values of a batch. The following sections explain
the steps involved.
Configuration Setting
You need to make the following two settings:
1. Go to SAP IMG  QM  Basic Settings  Maintain Settings at Plant Level  Inspection Lot
Completion  Transfer Inspection Results to Batch, and execute this program. The
system automatically activates the necessary settings.
2. Go to SAP IMG  QM  Basic Settings  Maintain Settings at Plant Level  Inspection Lot
Completion, and ensure that in the plant settings, the Batch Valuation without
Material Spec checkbox is selected. You may also go to Section 3.6.2 (Figure 3.88) for
this configuration setting.
Master Data Settings
The following is the master data that you need to maintain:
1. Create a class characteristic (Transaction CT04).
2. Create a batch class (Transaction CL01) of class type 023 (batch class).
3. Assign the newly created classed characteristic to the batch class at the time of batch
class creation (Transaction CL01).
4. Assign a batch class to the material master in the classification view (Transaction
MM01). Remember to use class type 023, which is specific to batch class.
5. Assign the inspection type in the material master (Transaction MM01). Choose
either inspection plan or material specification.
6. Create a master inspection characteristic with reference to the previously created
class characteristic (Transaction QS21).
7. Create an inspection plan with the previously created master inspection characteris-
tic (Transaction QP01) or create a material specification (Transaction QS61).
Note
We suggest that you also read Chapter 9, which explains how to create classes and
characteristics. Further, Chapter 9, Section 9.6, covers most of the master data settings
that you need to run this business process.
All examples in this book are for quantitative characteristics. But if you want to copy a
qualitative characteristic of an inspection lot to a batch classification, then while creat-
ing the class characteristic (Transaction CT04), go to the Values tab, choose Other

3 Quality Inspection
152
Value Check, and select the Catalog Char. radio button. Here, you can enter the
selected set and the associated plant.
Business Processes of Copy Inspection Results into Batch Classification
The business processes are as follows:
1. Create a manual inspection lot of lot origin 89 (Transaction QA01). In addition, create
a new batch number during inspection lot creation.
2. Record the results (Transaction QE01).
3. Record a usage decision (Transaction QA11). When you save the usage decision, a
message appears at the bottom of the screen to inform you about transfer of inspec-
tion results to batch classification.
4. Display the batch of the material (Transaction MSC3N). In the Classification tab,
you’ll find the inspection results transferred as batch characteristics.

sections.title: Usage Decision
sections.text:
3.2.5 Usage Decision
Let’s now cover the different types of usage decisions, including collective usage deci-
sions and automatic usage decisions:
 In collective usage decisions, several inspection lots that are already accepted during
the results recording processes are accepted via assignment of a single usage deci-
sion code (accepted) to multiple inspection lots.
 In automatic usage decision, the system reduces the time and effort required from
business users to record usage decisions of accepted inspection lots by automati-
cally assigning a usage decision code (accepted) to these inspection lots.
We’ll also cover how to reset a usage decision, as well as two ways of reversing one.
Collective Usage Decision
If you’ve inspected several inspection lots and found the results acceptable, then you
can release the material placed in quality inspection to the next processing step. It
makes sense to assign an accepted usage design code to all the accepted inspection lots
at once, instead of one at a time, saving you time and effort.
To perform a collective usage design, use Transaction QA16 or follow menu path Logis-
tics  Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Worklist  Inspection Lot Completion 
Collective Usage Decision (General) (see Figure 3.42).
Enter a specific inspection type, such as inspection type 89, so that the system displays
only inspection lots created manually. For the Usage Decision to Be Made area, enter
the UD Selected Set “UD89”, UD Plant “1710”, UD Code Group “UD89”, and UD Code “A”
(for accepted).
© 

153
3.2 Optimization Features of Inspection Planning and Quality Inspection
Figure 3.42 Collective Usage Decision: Initial Screen
Choose Execute (not shown) to go to the screen in Figure 3.43, which consists of a list of
quality inspection lots for which you can perform a collective usage design. You have
three options for performing collective usage design:
1. UD (Background)
The system performs all actions in the background; finally, a message appears at the
bottom of the screen to inform you when it saves the usage design code for the
inspection lot.
2. UD (Foreground)
You have to keep pressing (Enter) to validate each action that the system under-
takes. For example, you press (Enter) when the system selects the inspection lot,
incorporates the usage design code to the inspection lot, and prompts you to save
the changes made.
3. Manual UD
You select an inspection lot and manually assign the usage design code.
For this example, choose Inspection Lot 80000000353, and then choose More  UD
(Background). Once you successfully incorporate the usage design code, the system dis-
plays the message at the bottom of the screen that says Usage Decision for Lot 1710
80000000353 Is Saved.

3 Quality Inspection
154
Figure 3.43 Collective Usage Decision and Log
Let’s check out whether the system automatically and correctly assigns UD Code A to
Inspection Lot 80000000353. To view an inspection lot, use Transaction QA03, and
enter the inspection lot number, which in this example is “80000000353”. Figure 3.44
1 shows the display view of Inspection Lot 80000000353 with UD Code A automati-
cally assigned, and the long text 2 that the system automatically creates to maintain

Figure 3.44 Collective Usage Decision

Tips and Tricks
You can select multiple inspection lots in Figure 3.43 and perform a collective usage

Automatic Usage Decision
Consider a business scenario in which your reliable, long-time supplier routinely sup-
plies material that meets your company’s specification. To bring efficiency to the qual-
ity inspection process, as well as reward the supplier for reliably supplying quality
product, you can use automatic usage design functionality. Similarly, after a major
plant upgrade, the quality of the in-house-produced goods has greatly improved. In
this case, you repeatedly end up recording the same acceptable results of the inspected
material.
If the supplier regularly supplies satisfactory goods and all inspection lots are accepted,
then the company starts skipping the results recording step in QM until a problem in
any of the inspection lots arises. In the SAP system, these inspection lots have the SKIP
status. To optimize the entire business process in QM, you can perform an automatic
usage decision for all the inspection lots with the SKIP status, as follows:
1. In the plant settings, maintain the time lapse for automatic usage decisions. A time
lapse is the time that the system must wait before it proceeds with automatic usage
decision business process. See Figure 3.88 later in this chapter to see where you need
to maintain the requisite configuration settings.
2. You also need to ensure that the Automatic UD checkbox is selected in Inspection
Setup of the inspection type of the material-plant combination for which you want
to perform an automatic usage decision.
3. Use Transaction QA10 or follow menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality
Inspection  Worklist  Inspection Lot Completion  Automatic Usage Decision (Gen-
eral)  Trigger Manually to perform an automatic usage decision. For automatic
usage decision business processes, you need to ensure that the results recording
step of the inspection lots is complete and all characteristics are valuated and closed.
4. In Figure 3.45, enter Inspection Type “89” and Plant “1710”, and select both the Auto.
UD for Skipped Lots and Auto. UD for Completed Lots checkboxes.
5. For the Usage Decision area, enter the UD Selected Set as “UD89”, the UD Plant as
“1710”, UD Code Group as “UD89”, and finally Usage Decision Code as “A”. These set-
tings denote that the system assigns a usage decision code A (for “accepted”) from
the usage decision selected set 89, available in the plant 1710 and in the usage deci-
sion code group UD89.

3 Quality Inspection
156
Figure 3.45 Automatic Usage Decision
6. Choose Execute (not shown). The screen in Figure 3.46 1 appears, showing the log of
automatic usage decisions.
Figure 3.46 Log of Automatic Usage Decision

usage decision code A to inspection lots 890000000354 and 890000000355 2.

157

Note
Although this example covers manual steps for processing automatic usage decisions,
you can also have the system automatically perform this task for you via job planning
(as a batch job). To do this, use Transaction QA17 or follow menu path Logistics  Qual-
ity Management  Quality Inspection  Worklist  Inspection Lot Completion  Auto-
matic Usage Decision (General)  Job Planning.
On the initial screen that appears, create a variant and save it. In the second step of the
same initial screen, schedule how frequently you’d like the system to perform auto-
matic usage decisions. You can view the job planning overview with Transaction QA18
and check the complete log with Transaction QA10L.
You can also manually or automatically perform automatic usage decisions for produc-
tion, process, or plant maintenance orders. However, they must have completed/con-
firmed status before automatic usage decisions can take place.
To perform automatic usage decisions, use Transaction QA40 or follow menu path
Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Worklist  Inspection Lot Comple-
tion  Automatic Usage Decision (Order)  Trigger Manually. On the initial screen that
appears, enter the relevant plant, and then choose whether the order must be com-
pleted, only technically completed, or just confirmed for the system to perform auto-
matic usage decisions. You then need to assign a usage decision code to the inspection
lots for orders.
Reset Usage Decision
Sometimes, an incorrect usage decision is entered for an inspection lot, due to either
an incorrect manual data entry or an error made during collective or mass usage deci-
sions for quality inspection lots. Because an incorrect usage decision code leads to an
incorrect calculation of quality scores, it’s imperative that the user correct this anom-
aly as soon as possible.
To reset or change the usage decision code of an inspection lot, use Transaction QA12 or
follow menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Inspection Lot 
Usage Decision  Change with History. If you choose Reset UD, the existing usage deci-
sion code disappears. You can enter the new usage decision code at that time or do so
later. When you reset the usage decision, the system assigns the status UDRE to the
inspection lot. Upon resetting the usage decision code, you’re also able to change the
results of an inspection lot, if there’s any such business need. Changes to the previously
recorded inspection results aren’t possible if a usage decision for an inspection lot is
already made.

3 Quality Inspection
158
Tips and Tricks
If you can’t see the Reset UD option in your SAP system, you’ll need to engage an ABAP
resource who will implement and activate user exit QEVA0008.
Reverse Stock Posting
If you have an inspection lot that is stock-based, have your ABAP resource implement
user exit QEVA0008 to complete the reversal process. A stock-based inspection lot rever-
sal means that you’re resetting the usage decision code and placing the quality-cleared
inspection stock (unrestricted stock) back into quality inspection. Such business sce-
narios are applicable in goods receipt against a purchase order or a goods receipt
against a production or process order, in which you not only assign a usage decision
code to the inspection lot, but also simultaneously perform stock posting. The user exit
uses movement type 322 and transfers the quality-cleared stock back into quality
inspection stock. When implementing this user exit, you need to have a custom-
designed transaction to achieve the reversal objective. Your ABAP resource will be able
to manage this activity.
You can also use Transaction MIGO to reverse the material document even after a
usage decision for an inspection lot is made. The specific movement type is 101, against
which the system creates an inspection lot, which is for goods receipt for procurement.
The reversal of movement type 101 is 102. To perform the reversal, follow these steps:
1. From the first dropdown, choose Cancelation.
2. From the second dropdown, choose Material Document.
3. Enter the relevant manual documentation number that needs to be canceled.
4. Save your entries, and the system creates a material document number, which is
basically a reversal material document.
At the same time, the system brings the material’s stock quantity back into quality
inspection stock, and you can either put it into blocked stock or return it to the supplier
using the usage decision business process (Transaction QA11 or QA12).

The Engineering Workbench tool allows you to make mass changes to inspection plans

and for the allocation of PRTs to support QM.
The work area settings make it possible for you to adapt your inspections to the
special planning tasks in the QM area. A work area consists of a core and a working

environment. The core is the object type, based on which you make your selections.

3.3 Multiple Specifications
Multiple specifications attend to one of the critical requirements of the process indus-
try: to store specifications depending on freely selectable objects. Multiple specifica-
tions use the same fundamentals and basics that were previously covered in Chapter 2
in the material-routing assignment in the context of specific characteristic specifica-
tions. There, you can use different limits for various suppliers or customers in the same
inspection plan. Multiple specifications extend the scope of criteria that depend on the
material, suppliers, and customers. With multiple specifications, for example, custom-
ers often ask questions such as, “Does the tolerance limit of the active substance con-
tent of a supplier-delivered substance meet the approval in a selected country?”
The following example addresses the same question about the usage of a substance for
a specific country and covers not just the configuration basics or the master data that
you need to set up but also the business processes of multiple specifications.

sections.title: Dynamic Modification Rule
sections.text:
3.4 Dynamic Modification Rule
3.4 Dynamic Modification Rule
The dynamic modification rule eliminates the need to routinely record all inspection
results of every incoming raw material of a supplier or continuous manufacturing of
finished goods having acceptable quality. Integration of the dynamic modification rule
into procurement and production processes promises to bring about significant opti-
mization and efficiency. It skips a predefined number of inspection lots for results
recording purposes and requires a user to enter only a usage decision for the inspection
lots. However, a rejected inspection lot automatically triggers a normal or even tight-
ened inspection (see Figure 3.59). This ensures that necessary checks and balances are
in place, despite moving toward optimizing or automating some of the processes by
means of implementing the dynamic modification rule for reduced inspection efforts.
Figure 3.59 Dynamic Modification Rule at a Glance
In procurement, the dynamic modification rule helps to quickly bring the raw material
or packing material to the production line if the supplier adheres to the stringent qual-
ity control of the company. The dynamic modification rule provides for inspections at
periodic intervals. As soon as any problem in quality is observed, it reverts back to reg-
ular or tightened inspection until the supplier again meets the quality standards.
With the dynamic modification rule in place, the company benefits from reduced data
entry effort and is able to reduce the lead time to quality clear, which is in the time it takes
to process received goods in SAP S/4HANA and make them available to the production
process. It also helps to reduce inventory carrying costs. It enables suppliers to negotiate
better payment terms and a better selling price for their product, given that reliability
with the company has been established. Eventually, all these factors add up to a process
Time

Tightened
Normal
Reduced

Inspection

3 Quality Inspection
170
called annual or periodic supplier evaluation in SAP S/4HANA (see Chapter 19). Quality
plays a very important role in this process, in addition to price and timely deliveries.
This section covers the master data you need to set up the dynamic modification rule,
including sampling scheme and sampling procedure. This is then followed by the busi-
ness processes of the dynamic modification rule.
Note
Although this example covers integration of the dynamic modification rule into the
production process, the same principles apply to procurement processes.

sections.title: Master Data Maintenance
sections.text:
3.4.1 Master Data Maintenance
You need to make two quick checks of your master data to ensure that the dynamic
modification rule is effectively implemented when conducting transactions. The
checks are in the material master and master inspection characteristic, which we’ll dis-
cuss in the following subsections.
Material Master
The material has previously been created, but you need to activate its QM view at the
organizational level (plant). In addition, you need to activate inspection type 01 for
goods receipt against a purchase order. If the dynamic modification rule is imple-
mented in the production process, then make the relevant settings for inspection type
04 for process or production order.
Choose the Inspection Type detail for inspection type 01. Select the Skips Allowed
checkbox. This ensures that when the dynamic modification rule is working for inspec-
tion type 01, it allows skipping of inspection results recording. Inspection type 01 is
used to activate QM for goods receipts against a purchase order. Save your settings.
Note
If you intend to use the dynamic modification rule for goods receipt against the pro-
duction process, then you need to make the same Skips Allowed check in the material
master for inspection type 04. Inspection type 01 is the QM activation for goods receipt
for a purchase order or scheduling agreement with a supplier. You can also activate
this check in any other inspection type for which you want to integrate the dynamic
modification rule process.
Sampling Procedure in the Master Inspection Characteristic
You need to ensure that the Sampling Procedure checkbox is checked in the master
inspection characteristic. Just like the master inspection characteristic, the sampling
© 

171
3.4 Dynamic Modification Rule
procedure is also QM master data, and you use it to define the sample size of an inspec-
tion lot and how the system calculates it.
To change the master inspection characteristic, use Transaction QS23 or menu path
Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Inspection Characteris-
tic  Change. Choose Control Indicators, and select the Sampling Procedure checkbox.
Save your settings.
To effectively implement the dynamic modification rule in the production process,
maintain the QM master data in the sequence we’ll specify in the following sections.
Define a Sampling Scheme
In a sampling scheme, sample size is defined based on the total quantity of the goods
receipt. The sampling scheme also incorporates the information related to the number
of samples that can be accepted or rejected in a sample size to help decide whether the
quality inspector should accept or reject an inspection lot.
To create a sampling scheme, use Transaction QDP1 or menu path Logistics  Quality
Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Sampling  Sampling Scheme  Create. On
the initial screen, enter the sampling scheme (“QSS” in this example), and press (Enter)
to see the header data for the sampling scheme. Select the Valuation Parameters as
Attributive Insp. to ensure that the system automatically valuates all master inspection
characteristics within the tolerance limits as accepted and that the nonconforming
master inspection characteristics have the rejected valuation. Select the Sampling
Tables For as Severity/AQL.
Note
Acceptable quality level (AQL) is the international industry standard to define the total
percentage of samples that are either accepted or rejected from an overall sample cal-
culation. Hence, an AQL level of 3.5% allows defects of 3.5% of the overall sample size
calculation. If the system calculates the sample size of an inspection lot to be 100 and
its AQL is 3.5%, then not more than 3.5 samples out of the 100-sample lot can be
rejected for the system to consider the inspection lot as acceptable.
Although various international AQL standards, such as those of ISO, are available in
SAP as standard offerings and you can immediately begin using them, we’ll cover how
to create an AQL in detail, just in case there is a business need that is company-specific.
Choose Continue to define the inspection severity and AQL value. Choose the Inspec-
tion Severity dropdown, and the system brings up the four different severity levels.
Choose inspection severity 002, which denotes a reduced inspection; enter an AQL
Value of “3.000”; press (Enter) or choose QSS; and the screen in Figure 3.60 appears.

3 Quality Inspection
172
Figure 3.60 Sampling Table for Inspection Severity 2 (Reduced Inspection) and AQL Value of
2.000
Here, you see the sampling table for sampling scheme QSS with an inspection severity
of 002 and an AQL value of 3.000. Note that it’s standard SAP system behavior that all
leading zeros are eliminated, but up to three decimal places are shown. Therefore, in
Figure 3.60, the inspection severity of 002 has been changed to 2. Although the AQL
value is defined as 3.0 in Figure 3.60, the system shows up to three decimal places.
Here, define that the sample size is five units for an inspection lot quantity up to 500
units. Of that, a minimum of two units (column c1) has to be accepted, while a maxi-
mum of three units (column d1) is allowed for rejection. This is applicable for all the
inspection lots for which there is a reduced inspection. For an inspection lot of 10,000
units or more, the sample size is 10 units, while the number of acceptable samples is 4.
A maximum of 6 rejections is acceptable. Choose Other Table to go to the screen in
Figure 3.61.
The same process for creating another set for inspection severity and AQL is repeated
for an inspection severity of normal, which is denoted by 004 and with an AQL level of
4.000. This screen defines that for an inspection lot quantity of 500 units, there is a
sample size of five units, out of which a minimum of three units (column c1) has to be
accepted, while a maximum of four units (column d1) is allowed for rejection. For an
inspection lot of 10,000 or greater, the sample size is 10, and the number of acceptable
samples should be five. A maximum of seven rejections is acceptable. Save the sam-
pling scheme.
© 

173
3.4 Dynamic Modification Rule
Figure 3.61 Sampling Table for Inspection Severity 4 and Acceptable Quality Limit Value of
4.000
Depending on business requirements, there can be several variations for defining
reduced, normal, and tightened inspections in SAP S/4HANA. For example, with a
reduced inspection, there can be fewer sample sizes to inspect, while the acceptance
and rejection samples stay the same. In this example, we’ve kept the sample size for
reduced and normal inspection the same, which is 5 units for an inspection lot up to
500 units, but defined that for a reduced inspection, the acceptable samples should be
at least 2 units, and the maximum rejected samples should be 3 units. For a normal
inspection, at least 3 units must be acceptable, and a maximum of 4 units can be
rejected.
You can use the same process to define a tightened inspection. The produced good is
then monitored more frequently for quality checks until it’s able to maintain and sus-
tain the acceptable quality products over a longer period of time. Once this is achieved,
the tightened inspection can be brought back to normal inspection or even reduced
inspection. The option to define a tightened inspection with an inspection severity
code of 006 is defined. All subsequent steps remain the same as for reduced or normal
inspections.
Configuration Tip
To set up an inspection severity that meets your company’s business needs, follow the
configuration menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic
Data  Sample, SPC  Define Inspection Severities.

3 Quality Inspection
174
Setting Up a Sampling Procedure
A sampling procedure is the QM master data that helps you define how the system cal-
culates the sample size of an inspection lot. To create a sampling procedure, use Trans-
action QDV1 or menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic
Data  Sampling  Sampling Procedure  Create. On the initial screen of the sampling
procedure, define the sampling procedure (in this example, it’s “QMSP”) and press
(Enter) to bring up the screen in Figure 3.62, the assignments screen of the sampling
procedure. Here, assign the Sampling Type as Use sampling scheme, which you just cre-
ated in the previous step. Other sampling types available are Fixed Sample, which
entails that regardless of the inspection lot size, the sample size is fixed, and Percent-
age, which entails that the sample size is calculated based on a defined percentage of
the inspection lot.
For Valuation Mode, select Attributive inspection nonconf. units to ensure that the sys-
tem valuates a master inspection characteristic as accepted if the results are within the
specified tolerance limits. If any result is not, then the system valuates the master

sampling scheme QSS from which to choose—namely, reduced inspection with an AQL
of 3.000 and normal inspection with an AQL of 4.000.
Choose Reduced Inspection with an AQL value of 3.000, and then choose Continue to
go to Figure 3.64. Save your entries, and the system opens a popup that asks if you want
to create an allowed relationship between the sampling scheme and a dynamic modifi-
cation rule. As you have yet to create a dynamic modification rule that meets your
business needs, which we’ll cover in the next section, choose No in the popup.
Dynamic Modification Rule
The dynamic modification rule consists of user-defined rules that define the factors
that trigger a move from normal inspection to reduced inspection or vice versa. The
dynamic modification rule also enables you to define when the system should skip
results recording of inspection lots. The dynamic modification rule defines the number
of inspection lots that have the accepted or rejected statuses before the system
switches inspection stages from normal to reduced to tightened or vice versa.
To create a dynamic modification rule, use Transaction QDR1 or menu path Logistics 
Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Sampling  Dynamic Modification
Rule  Create. On the initial screen, enter “DMR” (in this example), and press (Enter).
On the header data screen for the dynamic modification rule, enter the short descrip-
tion, and select the dynamic modification rule as For Usage Decision. This option
ensures that the basis for the system to trigger the dynamic modification rule is a usage
decision of an inspection lot; that is, if an inspection lot has been accepted during the
usage decision, the dynamic modification rule decides whether there is a need for an
inspection stage change.
Warning
We suggest that you use the dynamic modification rule for usage decisions because, in
this case, the system only updates quality scores based on the usage decision, and in
the case of rejections and/or partial acceptance, the system updates the quality score
accordingly.
To use the dynamic modification rule at an inspection lot level, it entails that there will
be hardly any rejections, and the system updates the quality scores based only on
inspection lot creation. If you reject the material, the system doesn’t update the quality
scores, even though you run the cancellation process of the usage decision and results
recording.
©

3.4 Dynamic Modification Rule
Choose Continue to bring up the detailed screen to define inspection stages of a
dynamic modification rule (see Figure 3.65). An inspection stage enables the user to
define the number of accepted or rejected inspection lots that lead to an inspection
stage change. Inspection stages are also referred to as stages. For this example, there are
two stages: 1 and 2.
For stage 1, define an inspection severity of 2, which is the normal inspection. Also acti-
vate the ISt checkbox (initial stage) to ensure that the dynamic modification rule pro-
cesses always start with normal inspection (stage 1) before the stage changes to reduced
inspection (stage 2). In stage 2, activate the checkbox for Skip inspection, which means
that system allows skips in results recording for the inspection stage 2 (reduced inspec-
tion). Next, select the row of inspection Stage 1 shown in Figure 3.65, and choose Stage
Change. This leads to Figure 3.66.

stage 1. Here, define that at least one inspection lot must have the usage decision OK or
Accepted so that inspection stage 1 changes to stage 2. If there is a single rejection 1
with Not OK or a rejection in the Rejections field, then the next inspection stage is 1,
which is the normal inspection and requires results recording. Choose Continue, which
leads back to Figure 3.65.
Repeat the same process from the screen in Figure 3.65 by selecting Stage 2 and Stage
Change to go to the screen in Figure 3.66 2, which stipulates that there can be a maxi-
mum of two skips before the system considers stage change. If there is a skipped
inspection lot during results recording (for which no result recording is needed in the
first place), the system still creates the next inspection lot with the skip status on goods
receipt against the process order. Similarly, if there is one rejection (Not OK), then the
next stage remains 1, which is a normal inspection. In the case of infrequent inspec-
tions, you can define the maximum skip duration in days, after which the system must
take inspections into account. Choose Continue to go to the screen in Figure 3.67.
