3.4.2 Business Processes
Now that you’re familiar with the QM master data you need, let’s review the end-to-end
business process flow to show how the dynamic modification rule actually works. Cre-
ate a process order for the previously covered material for which the dynamic modifi-
cation rule is active, and perform its goods receipt. On goods receipt, the system creates
an inspection lot.
Use Transaction QA03 to display the inspection lot, which in this example is
10000000716 (see Figure 3.70). Notice that the dynamic modification rule applies
© 

181
3.4 Dynamic Modification Rule
successfully to inspection lot 10000000716. In addition, the system correctly calcu-
lates the sample size of 5 based on the goods receipt quantity of 100 PC.
Figure 3.70 Sampling Procedure and Dynamic Modification Rule in Inspection Lot
The next steps are to undertake results recording, followed by usage decision and stock
posting. For the usage decision, enter the acceptance code to accept the inspection lot
and undertake its stock posting. As soon as the usage decision is undertaken as an
accepted decision, further goods receipts against the same or different purchase order
have inspection lots with SKIP status. This means there’s no need for results recording,
and the usage decision alone is sufficient. The system denotes such an inspection lot
with the SKIP status. Figure 3.71 shows inspection lot number 10000000718, with the
SKIP status that the system assigned using the dynamic modification rule.
Tips and Tricks
If your organization needs to record results of an inspection lot with SKIP status, you
can still do so. The standard process of results recording prevails, although the system
issues an information message that a specific inspection lot has SKIP status.

3 Quality Inspection
182
Figure 3.71 Inspection Lot with SKIP Status
You can further check whether the dynamic modification rule setup is correct or com-
plete. Select two inspection lots with SKIP status, enter results, and then reject by
assigning a usage decision code as rejected for both inspection lots.
When you undertake subsequent goods receipt against the process order, the system
doesn’t trigger the dynamic modification rule with SKIP, and normal results recording
is required.
We just covered the functional aspects of dynamic modification rule functionality in
this section. However, Figure 3.72 shows the Quality Level History app, which leverages
the dynamic modification rule functionality to evaluate quality levels and history to
make more informed business decisions. The stage changes for the past several inspec-
tion lots are shown here.

3.5 New Inspection Types
In Chapter 2, we explained that creating new inspection types to meet business needs
normally doesn’t serve the purpose because the functions and functionality offered are
the same as you find with standard inspection types. However, in unique business sce-
narios, when you need to distinguish a quality inspection process from a routine or
normal inspection, you proceed with the necessary configuration of a new inspection
type and its associated dependent configuration that enables you to run the business
process.
The example in this section shows that you want to create a new inspection type to
attend to special inspection needs for tea leaves that come from specific tea gardens—
Darjeeling and Kenya gardens.
Here, you perform step-by-step configuration and assign the configured objects to
master data that lets you run the business process. Let’s get started.

2. Maintain the inspection type.

Create a Task List Usage
You’re already familiar with the concept of inspection types from Chapter 2. If an
inspection type is active, the system creates an inspection lot after a particular event,
even if there is no inspection plan yet. This event can be a goods receipt for the goods
movement for a purchase order or simply a manual inspection lot creation. When the
system creates an inspection lot, it looks for the relevant task list usage that you’ve
assigned in the inspection plan. You create a new task list usage to distinguish it from
your regular inspection or standard task list usage available in the system.

identify its usage; and stipulate that the task list usage will be available for material

material purchased, produced, or transferred when receiving the material in inventory.

This section covers configuration basics of quality planning and quality inspection.
Note
If you see a few configuration objects not covered in this chapter while navigating the

3.6.3 Quality Planning
The following sections will cover settings and options that you’ll find in the quality
planning configuration menu of QM.
Defect Classes
You may have different types of defect classes, such as critical or minor defects. You can
categorize the defects into different catalog types, such as quality defects or plant
maintenance defects. The SAP system characterizes defects into five different defect
class categories. You can choose to work with the defaults for defect classes or create
new ones.
To create defect classes, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality
Planning  Basic Data  Catalog  Define Defect Classes. Figure 3.89 shows an overview of
various defect classes. Choose Dfct Class 01 1 so that the detailed view of the defect
appears 2. The system displays the Quality Score. The critical or more severe a defect,
the lower the quality score. Together with the quality score in a defect class, the system
uses characteristic weighting to come up with an overall quality score of an inspection
lot, which forms the basis of supplier evaluation.
The system calculates the quality score based on the following equation:
Quality score = Quality score in defect class × Characteristic weighting ÷ Sum total of all
characteristic weightage
Batch Valuation Without
Material Spec.
Checkbox that requires characteristics in a batch to be
directly synchronized with material specifications so that
results recording can be successfully performed. This
option is helpful when you want to transfer inspection
results to batch classification. See Section 3.2.4, where we
put this option to use.
Field Details
Table 3.8 Inspection Lot Completion (Cont.)
© 

203
3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection
Figure 3.89 Defect Classes
If you select the Defect Class Allowed checkbox, the system offers the provision to
enter a defect class with defect codes, even though you’ve marked the valuation of the
characteristic as accepted. In other words, even the accepted master inspection charac-
teristic can still have defects, and this checkbox provides the necessary option to note
the same. Not choosing the checkbox only enables you to choose a defect class when
you have a rejected valuation of a characteristic.
The Next Functions in Results Recording area allows you to include the Workflow Link,
Activation Q-Notif., or No Next Function (or follow-up function) after recording a defect
class.
Define Defect Categories
With the define defect categories feature, you can define customer-specific defect cate-
gories for defects recording. The defect category controls the following settings:
 Using a customer-specific defect category, you can specify the task type for a defect.
The task type determines, for example, whether a follow-up action can be assigned
to a task in a defect.
 You can add context-specific fields for a defect category. This requires knowledge of
SAP Fiori elements.
 You can select defects of a customer-specific defect category via their defect cate-
gory in the Process Defects app.
To define a defect category, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Non-
conformance Management  Defects Recording  Define Defect Categories.

3 Quality Inspection
204
Catalogs
In the context of quality planning and quality inspection, the term catalog refers to a
collection of unique keys that describe a subject, both in the positive and the negative
sense. A catalog is a group of codes that you normally use to categorize different
aspects and activities of QM (and PM) and include defects, causes, tasks, actions, or
usage decisions. An example of a catalog of defects can be defect codes, which contain
all the possible defects of electrical or mechanical parts of the machinery.
In the SAP S/4HANA system implementation project, designing the defect catalogs and
other catalogs often takes significant time and effort because the existing catalog struc-
tures in the enterprise have to be migrated to a schema that suits the QM area. There-
fore, the most frequently occurring problem isn’t missing catalogs, but rather the sheer
number of catalogs and the fact that problem descriptions often overlap. The better-
suited and practical approach of classifying problem descriptions in catalogs according
to defect location, defect type, and defect cause also often causes uncertainty with
assigning the corresponding codes.
The following sections will discuss the various standard catalog types available in the
SAP S/4HANA system. Although standard catalog types available are generally suffi-
cient to meet most business needs, new catalog types can also be configured. Each cat-
alog type has specific codes that are then used in the business processes. Further, each
code within a catalog type provides an option to perform subsequent follow-on func-
tions too.
Catalog Types
You can select the defaults for catalog types or add additional ones if there is a business
need. To view the available catalog types, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Manage-
ment  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Catalog Types. Figure 3.90 shows the initial screen
of catalog types. You must not change SAP catalog types 1–9. However, you can create
new catalog types within the P–Z range.
The following catalog types are available in the SAP S/4HANA system:
 Catalog type 0: Action reasons
This catalog type is specific defects recording wherein specific action can be assigned
when a defect is first identified and recording.
 Catalog type 1: Characteristic attributes
This catalog type is specific to results recording and is for defining qualitative char-
acteristics. It has special importance in the catalog system. One reason for this is that
you can maintain both OK and NOK definitions here; another is that you can only
assess the catalog entries only via selected sets. If you’re using a rejected-defect class
for supplier evaluation, you have to enter a defect class (major defect, minor defect,
etc.). Rejecting defect classes are by nature the same as the defect types (defects) and
are structured in the same way. If a qualitative characteristic has been created in the
© 

205
3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection
inspection plan, the valuation always uses a code from the selected set of the charac-
teristic attributes.
 Catalog type 2: Tasks
You use this catalog to store the tasks that are necessary in the context of quality
notifications. Examples of typical tasks can include supplier visit, test equipment
calibration, construction change, or a process-capability test. You can also activate
automatic follow-up action functions here.
 Catalog type 3: Usage decisions
The system uses this special catalog type only for inspection lot completions. You
can only access this via selected sets. Every code in the selected set has further con-
trol functions that you can use to accept or reject valuation:
– Valuation (lot decision)
– Quality score
– Follow-on action
 Catalog type 4: Events
This catalog type contains events for PM.
 Catalog type 5: Causes
This catalog type is also used in quality notifications. Typical defect causes include,
for example, tool breakage, incorrect storage, transport damage, and incorrect deliv-
ery specification.
Figure 3.90 Catalog Types

3 Quality Inspection
206
 Catalog type 6: Effects
This catalog type contains the consequences of defects for PM.
 Catalog type 7: Hold
This catalog type contains the reasons to hold for PM.
 Catalog type 8: Activities (QM)
You define the actions to take as a result of measures. We recommend that you use
only measures in the quality notifications because it’s usually difficult to make a
clear logical distinction between measures and actions.
 Catalog type 9: Defect types
As with the characteristic attributes, you can assign defect classes to this catalog
type.
 Catalog type A: Activities (PM)
This catalog type contains the activities catalog for PM.
 Catalog type B: Object parts
This catalog type contains the object parts catalog for PM.
 Catalog type C: Overview of damage
This catalog type contains the damage catalog for PM.
 Catalog type D: Coding
This catalog type contains the general description that is used as the title or subject
of messages (error message, problem message, complaint, etc.). These entries are
also the titles for the error-description text.
 Catalog type E: Defect locations
The catalog structure is the same as the general definition.
 Catalog type F: Decision – SPM return
The catalog structure contains decision codes that the user can choose from while
deciding to return special machinery to the supplier (SPM).
Tips and Tricks
When the system displays the catalog entries in the results recording or in the quality
notifications, only the description of the code with its short text and key are visible. If
you also want the system to display the associated code group, enter “&” (an amper-
sand) in the code group text. The system inserts the code text into the code group text
in place of the & symbol.
To edit a catalog, follow menu path Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Inspec-
tion Lot Completion  Edit Code Groups and Codes for Usage Decisions. Figure 3.91
shows catalog 3 for usage decisions with code group 01. Within each code group, you
maintain individual codes and their descriptions.
© 

207
3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection
Figure 3.91 Catalog Type for Usage Decisions
Catalog Hierarchy
The catalog hierarchy usually has three levels, but in the case of catalogs with selected
sets, it has four. These are catalog types 1 (characteristic attributes) and 3 (usage deci-
sions), and they have an extra hierarchy level, known as selected sets. You can use this
extra level to group subsets of a code group according to higher criteria. In addition,
you assign an Accept or Reject valuation to every code in a selected set. You can also
assign a follow-up action to the individual codes.
To edit a selected set for usage decisions, follow menu path Quality Management 
Quality Inspection  Inspection Lot Completion  Edit Selected Sets for Usage Decisions.
Figure 3.92 shows catalog 3 (usage decisions) for plant 1710 and selected set 04 (goods
receipt). Notice that the first column is the code group of selected set 03, whereas the
second column is the individual code within the selected set. Each code of a selected set
can have a valuation code, such as Accepted (OK), Rejected (not OK), or Not Valuated. In
the Quality Score column, you can assign a quality score that is associated with each
code of a selected set. Referring to the Posting in UD column for a specific usage deci-
sion code of a selected set, you can leverage the system to automatically propose and
then take a necessary action based on the specific usage decision code for the selected
set for usage decisions. Figure 3.93 offers various options for Posting in UD that are
directly associated with the specific code of the selected set.
Tips and Tricks
Remember that you can assign UD Selected Set and its corresponding plant in an
inspection type so that during a usage decision, the system brings up only the relevant
usage decision codes for you to choose from. Refer to Section 3.4 for more information.

3 Quality Inspection
208
Figure 3.92 Selected Set
Figure 3.93 Stock Posting Options in Selected Set
Define Default Values for Control Indicators
The control indicator saves a significant amount of time and effort during master
inspection characteristic creation. During master inspection characteristic creation,
the user needs to select certain checkboxes. However, creating a control indicator and
then assigning it in a master inspection characteristic automatically enables all check-
box options.
While creating master inspection characteristics, look for the Preset Indicators field,
and then enter the code there.
© 

209
3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection
To define default values for control indicators, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality
Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Inspection Characteristic, Inspection
Method  Define Default Values for Control Indicators. Figure 3.94 shows the default
values indicator control key (IndCKey) 3010, where the right side shows the characteris-
tic control indicators. After you’ve made the necessary settings here, another popup
appears that allows you to incorporate more default values for the characteristic. You
assign this indicator control key 3010 while creating a characteristic.
Figure 3.94 Control Indicators
Define Characteristic Weighing
The system uses the characteristic weighing to calculate quality scores. A characteristic
with a critical defect will have a higher weight factor and will eventually have greater
impact on the quality scores calculation. In other words, a critical defect will lower the
quality score of the inspection lot. During results recording, if you record several
defects of an inspection lot, then the system multiplies each defect class’s score with
the weight factor to calculate an overall quality score for the inspection lot.

3 Quality Inspection
210
You can create characteristic weighing together with the weight factor by following
menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Inspection
Characteristic, Inspection Method  Define Characteristic Weighing. In the screen that
appears, choose Char. Wght 01, and the screen in Figure 3.95 appears. Checking the No
Skip Allowed checkbox ensures that, on selection of defect Critical Characteristic or
Charac. Weight 01, the system doesn’t allow inspection skips in results recording.
Figure 3.95 Characteristic Weighting
Define Inspector Qualification
An inspector qualification stipulates that a specific person or group requires the neces-
sary qualification to conduct the quality tests. Inspection qualification is for informa-
tion purposes only. It’s not a control function that can stop users from performing a
specific action. To define inspector qualification, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality
Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Inspection Characteristic, Inspection
Method  Define Inspector Qualification.
Define Tolerance Key
The tolerance key defines the tolerance range for the quantitative characteristic. When
the results of an inspection characteristic fall within the tolerance key/range, it’s
viewed as acceptable for the purpose of valuating the characteristic.
To create or change a tolerance key, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management 
Quality Planning  Basic Data  Inspection Characteristic, Inspection Method  Define
Tolerance Key. The screen that appears consists of a long list of industry-standard toler-
ance keys that you can evaluate before proceeding to create new ones. Choose Toler.
Key (tolerance key) A10, and then choose Details to pen the screen in Figure 3.96.
Here, you can control the number of decimal places, as well as define the unit of mea-
sure of the tolerance key. You can also set and copy the Target Value while creating a
characteristic. Choose Nominal Values in the screen in Figure 3.96 to go to the screen in
Figure 3.97 where you can define both upper and lower nominal, specification, and
limit values, including the number of decimal places for each.
© 

211
3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection
Figure 3.96 Tolerance Key
Figure 3.97 Details of Tolerance Key A10
Define the Estimation Procedure for Fraction of Defects
In this step, you can define your own procedure to estimate the percentage of defective
material using the characteristic inspection results. The following are the fraction esti-
mates:

3 Quality Inspection
212
 Nonconforming units (with regard to a characteristic and in the inspection lot)
 Characteristic values outside of the tolerance range
The keys for the procedure are defined in the inspection characteristic. The system
maintains fraction estimates for the following distributions:
 Binomial distribution
The system uses binomial distribution when there are exactly two mutually exclu-
sive outcomes of a result. The outcome is either a success or a failure.
 Poisson distribution
The Poisson distribution uses the model of number of events occurring within a
given time interval.
 Normal distribution
Mean and standard deviations are taken into account in a sample’s results.
To define an estimation procedure for a fraction of defects, follow menu path SAP IMG 
Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Inspection Characteristic, Inspec-
tion Method  Define Estimation Procedure for Fraction of Defects. In Figure 3.98, you
can define your own estimation procure and assign the relevant function module.
Figure 3.98 Share Estimate for Inspection Characteristics
Number Ranges
You can define your own number ranges for inspection characteristics and inspection
methods. To do this, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Plan-
ning  Basic Data  Inspection Characteristic, Inspection Method  Define Number Range
for Inspection Characteristics.
© 

213
3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection
The initial screen for Number Range for Inspection Characteristics appears. To add a
number range, choose Insert, and in the popup that appears, enter the identification
number (No), and then define the number range in From No. and To Number. You can
have internal and external number assignments. For the external number assignment
option, select the Ext checkbox.
Note
The basics of creating and assigning number ranges are the same, so you can use the
information in this section to create and assign them in other QM master data setups.
Inspection for Goods Movements
If you want to control inspection at procurement or transfer, you need to define it in
this configuration step. The SAP system has already defined this for standard move-
ment types. Only if you create a new movement type do you need to add it here. You
also need to make sure the inspection type is assigned to the inspection lot origin. Fur-
ther, if you want to control automatic creation of inspection lots for any movement
types, you can activate/deactivate them.
To make the necessary settings for inspection for goods movements, follow menu path
SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Inspection Lot Creation  Inspec-
tion for Goods Movement. In the popup that appears, choose Update Control, and then
enter your custom-defined movement type. Choose Back, and when the popup reap-
pears, choose Deactivate Quality Inspection for a Movement Type. This leads to Figure
3.99 where you can deactivate the QM function for any movement type(s) by selecting
the QM not active checkbox for the relevant movement type.
Figure 3.99 Deactivating QM for Movement Type

3 Quality Inspection
214
Note
In Appendix A, you’ll find a list of several movement types and associated inspection
origins. You can use that list to integrate QM into as many business processes as neces-
sary to meet your business needs.
Adapt Rules for Sample Determination
If the standard sampling procedure doesn’t fulfill your company’s business needs, then
you can assign additional or different rules by assigning a specific function module to
the sample determination rule. Use the menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management 
Quality Planning  Basic Data  Sample, SPC  Define Sampling Determination  Adapt
Rules for Sample Determination.
Define Valuation Mode
Valuation mode enables the system to valuate inspection characteristics based on
whether the mode of valuation will be manual or automatic and is for attributive (qual-
itative) or variable (quantitative) characteristics. When you’re creating a sampling pro-
cedure, you need to choose the relevant valuation mode that’s directly linked to the
valuation rule. Let’s explain this with an example.
Consider valuation mode 110 (Attr. Insp. Nonconforming Units/Manual), which con-
tains valuation rule 111 (Attr. Insp. Nonconforming Units/Manual). The combination of
valuation mode 110 and valuation rule 11 means that the system decides to accept or
reject an attributive (qualitative) characteristic based on how many of the inspected
samples of an inspection characteristic fail. For example, say that the total number of
samples inspected is 20 units, and you record 3 units as rejected due to defects or non-
conformance. Whether that characteristic passes or fails depends on the formula used
for valuation rule 11 or function module QEBR_NONCONFORM_UNIT_OR_MANUAL. You’ve
defined the actual number of samples allowed for pass or fail in the sampling proce-
dure. In this specific case, though the system automatically valuates the characteristic
as either accepted or rejected, it also provides an option for the user to manually valu-
ate or overrule the automatic valuation. This option to perform manual valuation
(despite the system’s automatic valuation) isn’t available if you use valuation rule 10.
To summarize, a few valuation modes are valuation by number of defects, number of
nonconforming units, or defect code, and they are for attributive or variable character-
istics with the option of automatic, manual, or both valuation controls of an inspection
characteristic.
Tips and Tricks
If the characteristic is quantitative, then choose a valuation mode in the sampling pro-
cedure as one of the variable types.
© 

215
3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection
If the characteristic is qualitative, then choose a valuation mode in the sampling proce-
dure as one of the attribute types.
To navigate to the valuation mode, use menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management 
Quality Planning  Basic Data  Sampling, SPC  Define Valuation Rules. In the screen that
appears, choose Valuation Mode 100.
You’ll see a screen that shows valuation mode 100 for attributive (qualitative) inspec-
tion by number of nonconforming (or number of defects) units, with valuation rule 10
assigned to valuation mode 100.
Define Valuation Rule
To set up or navigate to a valuation rule, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management 
Quality Planning  Basic Data  Sample, SPC  Define Sampling Determination. In the popup
that appears, choose Modify Valuation Rule, and then from the list of various available valu-
ation modes, choose Valuation Rule 10. This leads to the screen in Figure 3.100, wherein the
system uses the function module to valuate a characteristic.
Figure 3.100 Valuation Rules

3 Quality Inspection
216
If you have any unique business need to valuate a characteristic that’s not available in
the standard system offering, then you can create a function module and assign it in
this step.
Statistical Process Control
Organizations use the statistical process control as a tool to improve product quality by
reducing process variations. There are two sources of process variation:
 Chance variation (later renamed to common cause variation) that is inherent in the
process, stable over time, and assignable
 Uncontrolled variation (later renamed to special cause variation), which is unstable
over time—the result of specific events outside the system
Control charts attempt to distinguish between these two types of process variation:
 Common cause variation, which is intrinsic to the process and will always be present
 Special cause variation, which stems from external sources, indicates that the pro-
cess is out of statistical control, and needs evaluation on a case-by-case basis
When you create an inspection characteristic, you select the SPC checkbox to let the sys-
tem know that you’ll be monitoring this specific characteristic through the statistical
process control. In addition, remember to simultaneously select the Sampling Proce-
dure checkbox; otherwise, the system deactivates the SPC checkbox that you previously
selected. Later, when you assign this statistical process control characteristic to an
inspection plan, the system prompts you to enter the sampling procedure, as well as the
statistical process control criteria.
To navigate to the statistical process control criteria settings, follow menu path SAP
IMG  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Sampling, SPC  Statistical
Process Control  Define SPC Criteria. In Figure 3.101, you’ll find several combinations of
task list characteristics that align with the material, supplier, customer, and even equip-
ment or the functional location of PM. Choose SPC Crit. 010 1, and the details appears
on the screen on the right 2.
Usage is the option to select a specific task list to use the statistical process control cri-
teria. In addition, the radio buttons enable selection of the assignment of the control
chart either on every inspection lot or at every inspection point.
Note
See Chapter 19 on quality control to understand how to leverage statistical process
control to improve your business processes.
© 

217
3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection
Figure 3.101 Statistical Process Control Criteria
Define Control Chart Type
Control charts are most commonly used in the production area. Your system comes
with several preset sampling procedures for statistical process control inspection
planning. To define your own statistical process control sampling procedure in the
SAP S/4HANA system, proceed exactly as you would for the lot inspection. The sam-
pling procedure input mask contains one extra attribute: the indicator for the inspec-
tion point. The inspection point control object allows you to set the inspection

3 Quality Inspection
218
interval—that is, whether the inspection is to be container-based, time-interval-
based, or event-based.
Define the following first:
 Sample type
Only a fixed sample is allowed.
 Valuation mode
Select the special valuation mode, statistical process control inspection. With this
setting, valuations of samples or characteristics use the action limits of the quality
control chart. A rejection occurs if the action limits are violated. If there aren’t yet
enough measurement values to calculate an action limit, the procedure switches to
manual calculation until the measured values are sufficient.
 Control chart type
You have to assign a control chart type for statistical process control sampling pro-
cedures. When you do so, the system checks whether the sampling procedure will
use inspection points or independent multiple samples. With independent multiple
samples, control chart types with samples are allowed; otherwise, control chart
types without samples are allowed.
In control charts with memory (moving average chart, mean-value chart, or moving-
range chart), the control variable isn’t restricted to the current sample. These control
chart tracks don’t support the statistical process control inspection valuation mode.
When defining the sample size, there are some quality aspects that you have to take
into account. If you want to use the sample size n = 1, you should ensure the following:
 There is no S track in the control chart you intend to use.
 The overall dispersion, and not the internal dispersion, is used to calculate the pro-
cess dispersion in the calculations for the action limits. The reason for this is that in
samples with the size n = 1, the standard deviation is always 0.
Tips and Tricks
In statistical process control inspections with measured recording, sample sizes from 3
to 10 are normal, with n = 5 the most commonly used value.
For quantitative characteristics, the original values of which don’t have a normal distri-
bution, you can select a larger sample size to use the central specification limit set of
the statistics, whereby the distribution of the mean values is almost normal. You can
then use Shewhart charts for the mean value, even if the distribution of the population
isn’t normal. The more the distribution deviates from the norm, the greater the sample
size should be.
The statistical process control criteria determine the update process for the control
chart and are controlled by function modules. Before the system creates a new control
© 

219
3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection
chart (during results recording), this system checks whether a suitable chart already
exists. The function modules are well documented and can be easily adapted to suit
your own needs. It’s also a simple matter to create a control chart for a characteristic or
supplier only.
The standard SAP system already contains the following function modules:
 QRKS_CHARACTERISTIC: Control chart for characteristics
 QRKS_INSPECTION_LOT: Control chart for characteristics or inspection lots
 QRKS_MATERIAL: Control chart for characteristics or materials
 QRKS_MATERIAL_CUSTOMER: Control chart for characteristics, materials, or customers
 QRKS_MATERIAL_MANUFACTURER: Control chart for characteristics, materials, or manu-
facturers
 QRKS_MATERIAL_SOLD_TO_PARTY: Control chart for characteristics, materials, or sold-
to parties
 QRKS_MATERIAL_VENDOR: Control chart for characteristics, materials, or suppliers
 QRKS_MATERIAL_WORK_CENTER: Control chart for characteristics, materials, or work
centers
 QRKS_PURCHASING_DOCUMENT: Control chart for characteristics or purchasing docu-
ments
 QRKS_SALES_ORDER: Control chart for characteristics or sales orders
Statistical process control defines which charts are available, how you process them,
and how you assign them to the processes.
To define or make changes to the control settings of a control chart, follow menu path
SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Sampling, SPC  Statis-
tical Process Control  Define Control Chart Type.
On the initial screen that appears, first choose Ctrl Chart Type “110”, and then choose
Details (not shown) and the screen in Figure 3.102 appears.
Figure 3.103 shows the control chart type 110, Shewhart chart for x-Bar. Here, you can

production, and maintenance objects (e.g., equipment or functional locations). A con-

tion before you can record the results of an inspection lot or an inspection point.
To create or change the identifier for an inspection point, follow menu path SAP IMG 

type to denote the specific use inspection point. The inspection points available are as
follows:

 1: Inspection point for equipment
 2: Inspection point for functional location
 3: Inspection point for physical sample

Engineering Workbench
The Engineering Workbench facilitates the modification or updating of a large number
of QM master data and associated objects to save time and reduce the chances of data
entry error. You can either create a new working area or modify the existing ones to
meet your business needs. A working area makes available all the different fields and
options that you’ll use while using the Engineering Workbench.

another user is working in the Engineering Workbench. Notice that you can activate

and see the classes and their associated characteristics. The Object dependencies find

advanced classification functionality.
When you complete an inspection lot after the completion of a physical inspection,
you may or may not make the usage decision. You’re determining the quality valuation
and updating the quality level. If you have links to a batch class, you can transfer
inspection results to batch specifications. Based on the usage decision, the system can
perform follow-up actions.
Note that short-term and long-term inspection completion are two separate steps. For
short-term inspection, you need to enter the results before making the usage decision.
For long-term inspection, you can enter the results even after the usage decision has
been made for an inspection lot.

3.6.4 Quality Inspection
You can set up catalogs for usage decisions based on your business needs. Catalog type
3 is for usage decisions. To implement any usage decisions, you need to first imple-
ment a quality score procedure, follow-up actions, and inventory postings. This section
covers these configuration steps.
Define Quality Score Procedure
You can set a default value for determining a quality score in the inspection type. To do
this, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Inspection
Lot Completion  Define Quality Score Procedure.
The screen that appears shows the available standard options. Chose Q-Score Procedure
01 to see the screen in Figure 3.108. Notice that a function module is assigned to under-
take the necessary calculation for the quality score procedure. The Permitted Share of
Scrap checkbox enables a certain percentage of defects to be considered during quality
scores calculation. The Relevant Insp. Chars field provides an option to define whether
the results of master inspection characteristics are considered for quality score calcula-
tion, especially if the master inspection characteristics are closed and valuated.

rejected and sending a standard email to SAP users in the SAP mailbox, among others.

Define Origins of Results Data

Define Parameters for Calculated Characteristics
In this step, you can define the formula parameters for the input values of calculated
characteristics. You can achieve this in the following two ways:
 The formula parameters directly reference the fields in the input characteristics.
 The formula parameters reference function modules, which calculate the values in
the fields of the input characteristics.
For example, to determine the difference between the mean values of two characteris-
tics or samples, you need mean values for either characteristics or samples as input val-
ues. Because these mean values are available in the characteristic record, you can give
reference to the corresponding fields in the input characteristics. But to determine how
many values for a quantitative characteristic are above a target value, you need a spe-

3.7 Summary
Quality inspection entails following a series of business processes that record complete
inspection results, record defects, and make usage decisions that may or may not
include stock posting. When these business processes begin to mature and stabilize,
you can optimize some or all of them by automating them to reduce or eliminate
redundant data entry. Digital signature functionality brings greater business controls
and transparency to business processes. Dynamic modification rules enable a com-
pany to adjust quality levels based on the quality of products produced in house or
materials delivered by suppliers. Multiple specifications functionality offers far greater
flexibility in adapting to specific business needs of companies and span beyond a
material’s customer or supplier assignment.
The next chapter discusses how the QM functionality in SAP S/4HANA integrates with
the materials management functionality.
